claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally processed single-phase ZrB2 has high residual porosity and limited densification.
Adding a minor fraction of SiC to ZrB2 powder will lower its required sintering temperature.
Adding SiC will improve densification of the ZrB2 ceramic.
Improved densification will reduce hole formation during prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
SiC acts as a silicide-forming additive in the proposed ZrB2 processing route.
The additive-modified ZrB2 can be sintered near 2100–2200 °C.
A transient liquid phase or silicide bonding phase forms during sintering.
The transient or silicide phase enhances particle rearrangement and grain-boundary diffusion.
Enhanced particle rearrangement and grain-boundary diffusion produce a denser microstructure with fewer pores.
SiC reacts during sintering to form a silicide-rich intergranular phase.
The intergranular phase lowers the energy barrier for densification and accelerates mass transport.
Accelerated mass transport fills residual pores.
The denser microstructure resists corrosive attack and penetration by the plating liquid.
Resistance to plating-liquid attack and penetration mitigates hole formation and component failure.
The additive-modified material will achieve full densification at a sintering temperature approximately 100–200 °C lower than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
After long-duration plating-bath exposure, the additive-modified material will have fewer and smaller holes than conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
The additive-modified material will retain better structural integrity after plating-bath exposure.
Processing near 2100–2200 °C can provide the proposed benefit without compromising phase purity.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires that phase purity not be compromised, while the proposed mediator and mechanism require formation of a distinct silicide-rich intergranular or liquid phase. The intended meaning of phase purity is therefore internally inconsistent or insufficiently qualified.

The experiment says both sets are sintered under identical conditions but assigns the reduced 2100–2200 °C treatment specifically to the experimental set, while the baseline is conventionally processed above 2300 °C. The control temperature and whether temperature is held constant are consequently contradictory or ambiguous.
